title: Verdejo
description: Rueda's grape: herbal, citrus and fennel, with a bitter almond finish.
L: Verdejo gives crisp whites with lemon, grapefruit, green apple, fennel, bay leaf and fresh-cut grass, and a typical bitter almond finish. Acidity is medium to high, body light to medium. It's one of Spain's most popular whites, made mainly in Rueda, in Castilla y León.

Verdejo has grown in Rueda for centuries, probably brought from North Africa in the Middle Ages. It was long used for oxidised, Sherry-like wines. In 1972, the Rioja house Marqués de Riscal began making fresh, crisp Verdejo in Rueda, with cool fermentation. That modern style made Rueda famous; it became a DO in 1980.
What changed Verdejo's style in the 1970s?
Marqués de Riscal's fresh, cool-fermented wines
Riscal's modern approach created the fresh style Rueda is known for.

Look for pale lemon-green colour, citrus with herbal fennel and grassy notes, a crisp palate and a slightly bitter, almond finish. It's similar to Sauvignon Blanc, with which it's often blended, but more herbal, less pungent and with that bitter twist.
Verdejo was once used for oxidised, Sherry-like wines.
Yes. Before the 1970s, Rueda was known for oxidative styles.
Verdejo gives citrus, fennel and a bitter almond finish
It's grown in Rueda for centuries

Rueda lies on Spain's central Meseta, at 700 to 850 m. Its climate is continental: hot days, cold nights, harsh winters. Soils are stony, sandy and gravelly, with lime. The large day and night swing preserves Verdejo's acidity and aroma. Old ungrafted vines still grow in sandy soils.

Because Verdejo oxidises easily, many producers harvest at night, by machine, when temperatures are cooler. Cool grapes reach the winery fresh, keeping aromas. Skin contact and lees ageing can add texture. Most is made in steel; some top wines use oak or concrete eggs.

Know how long to keep it

Verdejo suits tapas, grilled fish, prawns, salads, goat's cheese and dishes with herbs. Its herbal notes match green sauces and fennel; its acidity handles fried food like calamari. In Castilla, it's the everyday white with lunch.
Serve at 7 to 9 degrees. Most Verdejo is best within one to two years. Oak- or lees-aged versions, and Rueda Dorado, a traditional oxidative fortified style, can age longer.
Its acidity cuts through fried food.
Rueda Dorado, a rare traditional style aged in glass demijohns in the sun and then in barrel, shows Verdejo's oxidative past.
